What is pure-roast (rang mộc) coffee?

Rang mộc means roasting coffee beans with nothing else: no butter, sugar, rice wine or flavorings. All the flavor in the cup comes from the beans and the roast.

Pure roast vs. butter-roasted Vietnamese coffee

A lot of Vietnamese ground coffee is "tẩm" during roasting: butter, sugar, rice wine, salt or flavorings are added so the beans look glossy, the brew is thick and black, and the aroma is strong. Some is also mixed with roasted corn or soybeans. Many people love that familiar taste, but it also hides the real quality of the beans.

Pure-roast coffee adds nothing. You taste the bean itself: fragrant, bright Arabica, or bold Robusta with a gentle bitterness and sweet finish.

Pure roast (rang mộc)Butter-roasted / mixed
BeansNatural brown, little shine (unless very dark)Glossy black, very even
SmellNatural roasted-coffee aromaStrong butter, vanilla or caramel scent
GroundsLoose and fluffy, don't stick to fingersClump and stick to fingers
Brewed coffeeBrown and clearBlack, thick and syrupy
TasteGentle bitterness, maybe light acidity, sweet finishHarsh bitterness or unusual sweetness

How to spot pure-roast coffee

  • Read the bag: pure-roast coffee usually states the beans, the blend ratio and the roast date.
  • Smell it: a soft, natural aroma, not a sharp perfume.
  • Look at the brew: browner and clearer than butter-roasted coffee.
  • A popular trick: sprinkle some grounds into cold water. Pure coffee tends to float and colour the water slowly; grounds mixed with grains often sink fast and cloud it. It's folk wisdom, not a replacement for clear information from the seller.
